opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question. When you ask a single diffusion model to generate a scene with, say, four or five people, you're asking it to solve many problems at once. It has to get each person's identity right: their face, their clothing, their body proportions. It also has to handle the relationships between them: who is standing where, who is in front of whom, how they interact, whether they're making eye contact or shaking hands. On top of that, the scene itself needs consistent lighting, perspective, and a plausible background.

These models learn from data, and most of that data is dominated by images with one or two prominent subjects. As the number of people grows, the combinatorial space explodes, and the model's internal representation starts to blur things together. That's why you see attribute leakage, where the red shirt you asked for on one person ends up on another, or faces that look like a blend of two people. You also see the familiar extra limbs and merged hands where two bodies overlap. The cross-attention mechanism that ties words in the prompt to regions in the image just isn't precise enough to keep every subject cleanly separated.

So my view is that it's more natural to decompose the problem, the way a human artist or a film crew would. First you reason about the layout: where each person goes and roughly what pose they're in. Then you generate or refine each individual with their own identity and attributes, and finally you compose and harmonize everything so the lighting, shadows, and occlusions are coherent. Breaking it into stages, or having several specialized components cooperate, gives you control and consistency that a single monolithic model struggles to deliver. It also makes the system easier to correct. If one person looks wrong, you fix that piece instead of regenerating the whole scene and hoping for the best.

r001.rationale: The response says one model must solve many problems at once, including people’s appearances, scene layout, interactions, and coherent lighting.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes reasoning about who stands where, occlusion, and how people interact.

r003.rationale: It mentions getting each person’s identity right, but does not clearly distinguish preserving specified people’s identities from generating arbitrary people.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it comes down to what a single model is actually being asked to do in that case. When you say "a crowded street with several people," you're not asking for one thing. You're asking for a composition problem, a layout problem, a problem of each individual being plausible on their own, and then a problem of all those individuals being consistent with each other and with the scene. That's a lot of distinct objectives to fold into one denoising process.

What we see in practice is that diffusion models are quite good at the dominant subject. If there's one person in the frame, the model allocates most of its capacity to getting that person right, and it does a nice job. But as soon as you have four or five people, the attention gets diluted. You start getting shared faces, duplicated limbs, people whose bodies merge at the edges, hands that belong to nobody. The model has learned a strong prior for "a person," but not a strong prior for "this specific person, in this position, distinct from the one next to them."

Part of the reason is the training data. Most captions describing images with multiple people are very coarse. They say "a group of friends at a party," they don't say where each person stands, what each one is wearing, what each one is doing. So the model never gets the supervision it would need to learn fine-grained control over multiple instances. It learns the gestalt, not the parts.

And then there's the text encoder bottleneck. You're squeezing a long, structured description into a fixed set of tokens, and the binding between attributes and subjects gets lost. "A woman in red next to a man in blue" very easily becomes two people in purple, or two people in red.

So my view is that asking one monolithic model to resolve all of that in a single pass is asking it to be a layout planner, a renderer, and a consistency checker all at once. It's much more natural to decompose the problem. Have one stage that decides the arrangement, where each person goes, how big they are, what they're doing. Then have the generation conditioned on that, perhaps even region by region, so each individual gets the model's full capacity. And then a stage that harmonizes everything, lighting, occlusion, interactions between people. You end up with something that looks a lot more like a pipeline than a single model, but that's really how the problem wants to be structured.

r001.rationale: It says a single model must solve composition, layout, individual plausibility, and consistency in one denoising process, making the task too demanding.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says the people must be consistent with each other and describes harmonizing their interactions.

r003.rationale: It discusses making each person distinct from neighbors, but does not clearly distinguish preserving the identities of specified people from generating arbitrary people.

astra-6.text:
Well, think about how many things the model has to get right at the same time. Each person has a pose, an appearance, and a position in the scene. Then there are relationships between people: who is looking at whom, who is standing behind someone else, or whose hand is holding an object. All of those details need to be consistent.

So the challenge is not simply generating several convincing people. It is composing them into one coherent scene while keeping their attributes and interactions separate. A single model has to solve all of those constraints together, and that becomes increasingly difficult as you add people. That’s why it can make sense to break the problem into smaller pieces, with some mechanism coordinating the overall composition.

r001.rationale: It says a single model must solve the people’s attributes, positions, and interactions together, becoming more difficult as people are added.

r002.rationale: It explicitly identifies relationships such as who looks at whom, who stands behind someone, and whose hand holds an object.

r003.rationale: It mentions keeping attributes separate, but does not distinguish preserving specified people’s identities from generating arbitrary people.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, think about how much has to be coordinated. The model has to generate each person with a plausible pose and appearance, but it also has to get the relationships between them right: who is looking at whom, who is in front of whom, how their bodies overlap, and how they interact with objects. All of that has to be consistent with the same perspective and lighting.

So it’s not simply generating one person several times. Every additional person introduces more constraints between different parts of the image. A model can produce something that looks convincing overall while still mixing up which hand belongs to which person or which person is performing an action. That’s why it may make sense to break the problem into smaller pieces, with an explicit representation of the scene to coordinate them.

r001.rationale: It says a single model must coordinate each person’s pose and appearance along with multiple cross-image constraints, and suggests breaking the task into smaller pieces.

r002.rationale: It explicitly names relationships such as who looks at whom, who is in front, body overlap, and interactions.

r003.rationale: It discusses generating people and coordinating their relationships, but does not distinguish preserving specified identities from generating arbitrary people.
